LABEL: abductive reasoning
DEFINITION: A form of logical inference in which a hypothesis is created about the probable causes from observed patterns.
EXAMPLE: Data mining is essentially an abductive process.
NOTE: Abductive reasoning is the primary source of new knowledge.

LABEL: abstract
DEFINITION: A more generalized representation.
EXAMPLE: "Animal" is a more abstract concept than "bear."

LABEL: accretion
DEFINITION: The process of gradual change, which is typically accommodated by a system structure.
EXAMPLE: In nature, the depositing of silt on a river bend is an accretive change. Overflowing the bank and creating a new channel is an avulsive change.

LABEL: acyclic
DEFINITION: Not cyclic; does not loop recursively.
EXAMPLE: If you were one of your own ancestors, you would have a cyclic family tree.

LABEL: agent
DEFINITION: An autonomous software program acting on a user’s behalf.

LABEL: aggregate
DEFINITION: A type of relationship that implies ownership.
NOTE: Aggregate relationships are used in the Unified Modeling Language (UML) and entity-relationship (ER) diagrams.

LABEL: alias
DEFINITION: An alternative and usually easier-to-understand name for a defined data object.

LABEL: alias
DEFINITION: An alternative name for something.

LABEL: ambiguity
DEFINITION: A definition or identification that can be understood in more than one way.
NOTE: Ambiguity leaves uncertainty as to the specific assignment of referent to thing.

LABEL: annotation
DEFINITION: The addition of qualifying or contextual information to text or an interface description.

LABEL: annotation
DEFINITION: A property that is not interpreted by the inference engine.
EXAMPLE: Annotations can include comments plus a large number of other properties that could be interpreted by other processors.

LABEL: antonymy
DEFINITION: A sense relation between two words with opposite meanings.
EXAMPLE: "Light" and "dark," "dead" and "alive," "slow" and "quick" are pairs of antonyms.

LABEL: assertion
DEFINITION: A statement that asserts that a certain premise is true.
EXAMPLE: "Robert Jones is Employee 1234" or "the Earth is round" are assertions.

LABEL: assertional box
DEFINITION: Inferences on instances (assertions).
EXAMPLE: Essentially reasoning on instances, similar to the way SQL reasons over instances in a database. Also, extensional.
NOTE: TBox statements are sometimes associated with object-oriented classes and ABox statements associated with instances of those classes.

LABEL: association
DEFINITION: A type of relationship that does not imply ownership.

LABEL: associative database
DEFINITION: A style of database design, using sentences to describe associations.

LABEL: asynchronous messaging
DEFINITION: Message transmissions without a “block and wait” for response.

LABEL: Atom
DEFINITION: An ontology for describing RSS feeds in XML.

LABEL: attribute
DEFINITION: A property or characteristic of an entity.
NOTE: An attribute is not a property in terms of a relationship expressed in RDF. In other words, an attribute does not connects two concepts.

LABEL: axiom
DEFINITION: A statement of self-evident truth used as a starting point for reasoning.

LABEL: behavior
DEFINITION: The methods that execute code.

LABEL: binary
DEFINITION: A relationship with an inverse.

LABEL: bind
DEFINITION: Attaching a request to an implementation. Implementations are in specific technologies, and to invoke them one has to attach an often abstract description of a request to the specific module that will invoke it. Adaptors bind to applications.

LABEL: Business Process Execution Language
DEFINITION: A standard for assembling a set of discrete web-based services in a service-oriented architecture into an end-to-end process flow.

LABEL: canonical
DEFINITION: An accepted standard.
NOTE: In message modeling, declaring something "canonical" is the process of declaring a standard for message content rather than allowing each project to define its own.

LABEL: cardinality
DEFINITION: A constraint on the number of successors on a relationship.
EXAMPLE: The cardinality for the relationship "biological mother" is 1; for "biological child" it is 0 or greater.

LABEL: cardinality
DEFINITION: A type of class restriction that limits the members of a class to those with the requisite number of unique property assertions.

LABEL: categorization
DEFINITION: The act of ascribing an instance to a knowledge-level group for the purpose of inferring additional information about the instance.

LABEL: causation
DEFINITION: A relationship with teleologic attribute.
EXAMPLE: Travel causes displacement.

LABEL: character data
DEFINITION: Character data that is ignored by a parser.

LABEL: class
DEFINITION: A definition of attributes and behaviors for a type of instance; the basic module for object-oriented programming.
NOTE: In object-oriented programming, "class" and "type" are nearly synonymous, but the slight difference causes considerable problems.

LABEL: co-occurrence analysis
DEFINITION: Using contiguousness as a clue for evaluating the relatedness of things.
EXAMPLE: If two terms typically show up near each other in text, they are likely related.

LABEL: cohesion
DEFINITION: The degree to which the elements inside a module belong together.
EXAMPLE: In a cohesive module, all the parts are closely related; there are no extraneous parts.

LABEL: column
DEFINITION: An attribute for relational databases.

LABEL: commitment to ontology
DEFINITION: Declaration that a domain or document makes in terms of using and agreeing with the meaning of terms from a particular ontology.
NOTE: The commitment to ontology is the key to different documents being able to intercommunicate.

LABEL: common logic
DEFINITION: Framework for a set of knowledge representation standards.

LABEL: competency question
DEFINITION: A question that defines the objective, scope and expressiveness requirements for an ontology.

LABEL: complete
DEFINITION: A class that has necessary and sufficient conditions; a restriction class.

LABEL: compound
DEFINITION: Group of individual words whose meaning can only be known in combination.
EXAMPLE: World Series, the White House

LABEL: conceptual model
DEFINITION: Model independent of implementation.

LABEL: conceptualization
DEFINITION: Abstract, simplified view of the world that we wish to represent for some purpose.

LABEL: conjunction
DEFINITION: And.

LABEL: consortium
DEFINITION: An association, typically a group of business companies.

LABEL: constraints
DEFINITION: Predicates which must be true or else transactions are not committed.

LABEL: content
DEFINITION: Intellectual property.
EXAMPLE: Documents, messages

LABEL: controlled vocabulary
DEFINITION: Pre-defined list of allowable terms with definitions.

LABEL: Cyc
DEFINITION: From encyclopedia, a project to capture and express the axioms needed for a machine to reason equivalently to a human.

LABEL: Cyc
DEFINITION: An ontology built by Cycorp to support common sense reasoning.

LABEL: CycL
DEFINITION: Inference language used in Cyc.

LABEL: DAML+OIL
SYNONYM: DARPA Agent Markup Language, Ontology Inference Layer, Ontology Interchange Language
DEFINITION: A successor language to DAML and OIL that combines features of both.
NOTE: DAML+OIL is superseded by the Web Ontology Language (OWL).

LABEL: DARPA Agent Markup Language
DEFINITION: Pre-OWL extensions to RDF to create ontologies for the Semantic Web.

LABEL: declared membership
DEFINITION: A class where the intention of the designers is to have users declare that instances/individuals are members of the class.

LABEL: deduction
DEFINITION: To infer knowledge of an instance from its membership in a category or type. The process of using knowledge but not of creating it.

LABEL: Defense Advanced Research Project Agency
DEFINITION: A funding source for the early Internet and currently the semantic web.

LABEL: definition
DEFINITION: A description of what something means.
NOTE: Definitions are often sufficient for humans, rarely sufficient for software agents.

LABEL: delimiters
DEFINITION: Separators in a message that allow a parser to know where one element starts and ends.

LABEL: dependency
DEFINITION: Recognition that one software component will be adversely affected if another one changes. Most software has dependencies on its operating system, but will also have dependencies of an often deep stack of other software components.

LABEL: derived membership
DEFINITION: A class where the intention of the designers is to have instances/individuals be assigned membership by a reasoning engine.

LABEL: description logic
DEFINITION: A specialization in computer science that uses formal language to define classes.
EXAMPLE: OWL/DL is a standard for describing Description Logic.

LABEL: description logic
DEFINITION: A form of formal logic that focuses on inference, which as been adopted by the Semantic Web in the form of OWL/DL.

LABEL: design time
DEFINITION: Refers to things that need to be changed when the software is being designed (or modified). For example, a scheduling algorithm is normally a design-time choice. However, it is possible to design an architecture in which the algorithm is a run-time option that could be selected by a user or another software component.

LABEL: dialect
DEFINITION: A subset of a language agreed to by a group of people.

LABEL: dictionary
DEFINITION: Place where metadata for the definition of tables, columns, and so on are stored.

LABEL: dictionary
DEFINITION: A collection of word definitions, with the purpose of distinguishing closely related words. Most dictionaries contain considerable encyclopedia functionality, which obscures their distinction function.

LABEL: dimension
DEFINITION: One of the axes in a data warehouse that can be used to query or summarize the facts in the warehouse.

LABEL: directed
DEFINITION: In a network model the property that says whether the arcs have "arrows." A project plan is "directed" in that the precedent relationships go in a particular direction. A thesaurus is undirected in that the definitions are only related, without having a direction to them.

LABEL: directed acylic graph
DEFINITION: Graph (network) in which all the nodes are connected and prevented from looping.

LABEL: directed graph
DEFINITION: A graph in which the arcs are directed.

LABEL: directory Mozilla
DEFINITION: Group of volunteers who categorize web sites.

LABEL: disambiguate
DEFINITION: Process of selecting between alternate, ambiguous interpretations. Conversationally, people do this by asking, "Do you mean x or y?"

LABEL: disjoint
DEFINITION: Two classes, sets or individuals can not have overlapping membership. Male and Female are disjoint.

LABEL: disjunction
DEFINITION: “Or.” The disjunction of two statements is true if either is true.

LABEL: distinction
DEFINITION: To set up rules for disambiguating closely related concepts.

LABEL: document-type definition
DEFINITION: Schema language for SGML, and XML.

LABEL: Dolce
DEFINITION: EU/Wonder Web sponsored Upper Ontology.

LABEL: domain
DEFINITION: The set of valid values of an attribute, i.e., its type. Note: this is very different form the ontology definition of domain below.

LABEL: domain
DEFINITION: A restriction on the classes that are the subject of a property relationship.

LABEL: Dublin Core
DEFINITION: Standard ontology for documents.

LABEL: element
DEFINITION: Atomic unit of meaning in XML.

LABEL: encyclopedia
DEFINITION: A description of what is known about a concept. This is distinct from distinguishing one concept from another, closely related, concept.

LABEL: entailment
DEFINITION: Semantic implication within a context, for example buying entails paying.

LABEL: enterprise application integration
DEFINITION: Industry and products involved in making the interfacing of applications more economical.

LABEL: enterprise information integration
DEFINITION: Architecture where federated queries are used to create an integrated view over many databases.

LABEL: enterprise message model
DEFINITION: A set of messages taken in the aggregate that represent the shared information in an organization.

LABEL: entity extraction
DEFINITION: Process of identifying concepts found in documents and tagging them to a predefined ontology.

LABEL: entity relationship
DEFINITION: Style of data design focused on the definition of entities and their relationship to each other.

LABEL: epistemology
DEFINITION: A branch of philosophy that studies the nature of knowledge.

LABEL: equivalent
DEFINITION: Two representations of the same thing.

LABEL: avulsion
DEFINITION: Rapid, discontinuous change; a change to a data structure that breaks dependent modules.
EXAMPLE: In nature, the depositing of silt on a river bend is an accretive change. Overflowing the bank and creating a new channel is an evulsive change.

LABEL: explicit
DEFINITION: A formal expression of knowledge.

LABEL: extensible
DEFINITION: Capable of being added to accretively. An extensible data structure is one that additive changes can easily be made. Relational databases are extensible at the table level, in that columns can be added to tables without requiring programs to be rewritten.

LABEL: extensible style sheet language transformation
DEFINITION: Extension to XSL that includes more structural changes to an XML document.

LABEL: extensional
DEFINITION: A set defined by a specific list.
EXAMPLE: The states of the United States is an extensional set.

LABEL: extreme programming
DEFINITION: First of the agile methods, focused on pair programming, test as you go, and refactoring.

LABEL: faceted
DEFINITION: Having the orthogonally distinct aspects of a taxonomy separated so that each can be dealt with independently.

LABEL: first order logic
DEFINITION: A branch of logic dealing with predicate-based reasoning.

LABEL: folksonomy
DEFINITION: A set of tags made up on the fly by end users to organize a body of work. Almost always a navigational taxonomy.

LABEL: formal
DEFINITION: A taxonomy where all the relationships are “isa” relationships, which can therefore be used in inference.

LABEL: friend of a friend
DEFINITION: An ontology about people and their properties.

LABEL: functional
DEFINITION: Characteristic of a property which guarantees that there is only a single object.
EXAMPLE: “BiologicalMother” is a functional property.

LABEL: generalize
DEFINITION: To create a more abstract definition or category.

LABEL: gist
DEFINITION: A minimal upper ontology.

LABEL: glossary
DEFINITION: A list of terms and their definitions.

LABEL: grammar
DEFINITION: A set of rules for ordering vocabulary items. In computer science, grammar may be expressed formally.

LABEL: granularity
DEFINITION: Size of the service. A service with a high level of granularity is referred to as being fine-grained and one with a low-level is coarse-grained.

LABEL: graph
DEFINITION: A model of entities (i.e., nodes) connected to relationships (i.e., arcs).

LABEL: grid
DEFINITION: A topology where large numbers of processors can contribute to solving one problem.

LABEL: grounding
DEFINITION: A connection of implication to empirical data. How we connect pure thought to the real world.

LABEL: hierarchy
DEFINITION: A tree-style arrangement of terms or classes in which each child has only one parent (i.e., single inheritance).

LABEL: homonym
DEFINITION: Two different meanings sharing the same word and the same spelling.
EXAMPLE: "Mogul" meaning the emperor versus "mogul" meaning the ski bump.

LABEL: hypernymy
DEFINITION: A word of a more specific meaning.
EXAMPLE: "Arabian" is a kind of "horse."

LABEL: hypertext markup language
DEFINITION: A tag-based language on which the World Wide Web is based.

LABEL: hypertext transfer protocol
DEFINITION: A standard request to Web servers; the protocol on which much of the World Wide Web is based.

LABEL: hyponymy
DEFINITION: Inverse of hypernymy.
EXAMPLE: ”Mammal” is a more general type than “horse.”

LABEL: identify
DEFINITION: To associate the description of an entity with its real-world counterpart.

LABEL: identity
DEFINITION: That which we perceive to be permanent about a perceived real-world entity; the identity of a person or an organization.

LABEL: idiolect
DEFINITION: Dialect spoken by an individual.

LABEL: individual
DEFINITION: An individual object as distinct from a type of object or class. This is often used synonomously with instance although that actually describes the membership of an individual in a class.

LABEL: induction
DEFINITION: Process of creating categories from instances. Probabilistic reasoning.

LABEL: inference
DEFINITION: Reasoning from known propositions.

LABEL: inference engine
DEFINITION: A software program that can assign members to classes based on formal class definitions.

LABEL: inheritance
DEFINITION: The accretion of properties and behaviors from a hyponym.

LABEL: instance
DEFINITION: Individual objects that belong to a class are referred to as instances of that class. Individuals can be instances of several classes.
EXAMPLE: e.g., Dave McComb is an instance of the class Person.

LABEL: instances
DEFINITION: Specific individual groups of data, usually created from some sort of template. In object-oriented systems, calling “new()” on a class creates an object that is of the type of the class. In a database system, inserting a row in a table creates an instance of that entity.

LABEL: instantiate
DEFINITION: The act of creating an instance of a class.

LABEL: intensional
DEFINITION: A set defined by rules. Each time the rules are executed you might get a different set. The set of customers with overdue balances is an intensional set. Opposite of extensional.

LABEL: intentional
DEFINITION: A programming language and style, where the “intention” of the developer is captured separate from the details of the implementation.

LABEL: inverse of
DEFINITION: For bidirectional relationships, the one that "goes the other way" ("child" is the inverse of "parent").

LABEL: isa
DEFINITION: Shorthand for the specialization/generalization relationship. Basis for inheritance in object-oriented design. See subsumption.

LABEL: isa
DEFINITION: Member of.
EXAMPLE: Dave (instance) isa Person (type or class). The two forms of isa are often confounded.

LABEL: Jena
DEFINITION: Open source Java-based framework built by HP Labs for building RDF-based Semantic Web applications.

LABEL: keyword
DEFINITION: To find content, we extract some of the less common words from a document and index them back to their location in the document.

LABEL: knowledge
DEFINITION: An agent has knowledge of a scenario or context to the extent that it has a model that provides some degree of predictability.

LABEL: knowledge interchange format
DEFINITION: A standard format for exchanging rules between AI systems.

LABEL: knowledge level
DEFINITION: Part of a model in which you reason about the behavior of the system rather than its implementation.

LABEL: lexical
DEFINITION: Having to do with words, as in a lexical analysis of text.

LABEL: lexicographer
DEFINITION: A person who writes dictionaries.

LABEL: lexicon
DEFINITION: Computer-readable dictionary of attributes.

LABEL: linguistic
DEFINITION: Pertaining to language.

LABEL: literal
DEFINITION: Constant variable (sounds like an oxymoron).

LABEL: mandatory
DEFINITION: In a relationship, a constraint that a particular relationship must have at least one successor.

LABEL: Markov
DEFINITION: Statistical algorithm for finding patterns and predicting similarity in unstructured documents.

LABEL: markup
DEFINITION: Annotating documents by inserting matching tags to offset certain sections.

LABEL: mashups
DEFINITION: Web-based user interface where integration is done in the browser using data from multiple sources.

LABEL: mereology
DEFINITION: The study of part-whole relationships.

LABEL: meronomy
DEFINITION: Terms related through a part-whole relationship.

LABEL: message
DEFINITION: Object-oriented design refers to a method call as a message, even though it is a function call.

LABEL: message
DEFINITION: The unit of work in an SOA, often serialized as XML.

LABEL: meta
DEFINITION: To transcend or go above. For most of computer science in means "about," as in “metadata is data about data."

LABEL: metadata
DEFINITION: Data about data. Includes data which describes how data is stored, where it is stored, how it is validated, and what it means.

LABEL: metametadata
DEFINITION: Data about metadata (usually at a high level of abstraction).

LABEL: metaphysics
DEFINITION: A branch of philosophy that deals with understanding the fundamental nature of everything, particularly the relationship of mind to matter.

LABEL: microformats
DEFINITION: An approach to embedding small bits of semantics in XML or XHTML.

LABEL: model-theoretic semantics
DEFINITION: An account of meaning in which sentences are interpreted in terms of a model of, or abstract formal structure representing, an actual or possible state of the world.

LABEL: namespace
DEFINITION: A domain within which a name is guaranteed to be unique and findable.

LABEL: natural language processing
DEFINITION: A branch of artificial intelligence that deals with interpreting and generating humanlike speech.

LABEL: navigational
DEFINITION: Non-formal taxonomies intended to aid users in finding information in a large source.

LABEL: node folding
DEFINITION: Process whereby a large number of independently defined “triples” are combined into a logical graph.

LABEL: nomenclature
DEFINITION: Set of names for terms in a given domain.

LABEL: nominalization
DEFINITION: To convert a verb to a noun. Used in software programs to create a handle for a method.

LABEL: normalization
DEFINITION: Arrangement of attributes to tables in a relational design so as to avoid update anomalies. Ensuring that each property is dependent only on the primary keys of its table.

LABEL: Notation 3
DEFINITION: Shorthand way of writing rules in Semantic Web.

LABEL: Notation3
DEFINITION: A shorthand way of writing rules in the Semantic Web.

LABEL: object oriented
DEFINITION: Style of programming that features data hiding within classes, and type and property inheritance.

LABEL: object role modeling
DEFINITION: Conceptual design notation focused on role modeling. Enables good modeling, especially for relationships of higher valence.

LABEL: ontology
DEFINITION: A subdiscipline of metaphysics which concerns itself with the nature of being.

LABEL: ontology
DEFINITION: A specification of a conceptualization.

LABEL: ontology inference layer
DEFINITION: Standard for defining and interchanging ontologies.

LABEL: orthogonality
DEFINITION: Literally "at right angles." Refers to finding aspects of categorization that are as independent of each other as possible.

LABEL: OWL-S Standard
DEFINITION: An ontology for describing the capabilities of Web services.

LABEL: parse
DEFINITION: To separate an incoming stream of data into its constituent parts based on a grammer and various delimiters.

LABEL: partial
DEFINITION: A partial class is one that has necessary, but not necessary and sufficient restrictions.

LABEL: partonomy
DEFINITION: A mereological hierarchy; a type of hierarchy that deals with part–whole relationships.
EXAMPLE: A bill of materials

LABEL: parsed character data
DEFINITION: Text that can be parsed.

LABEL: perception
DEFINITION: The process whereby humans discern order in a complex world.

LABEL: phenomenology
DEFINITION: A branch of metaphysics that reality consists of objects and events as perceived by human consciousness.

LABEL: polymorphism
DEFINITION: Literally "to take many forms." In object-oOriented design, subclasses of a class implement the public interface to the parent class in such a way that a message sent to a collection of parents and children would be responded to by each appropriately, without the caller knowing.

LABEL: polysemous
DEFINITION: A word with multiple related meanings.
EXAMPLE: Mouth, the anatomic opening, and mouth, the opening of a cave.

LABEL: pragmatism
DEFINITION: A branch of philosophy that holds that both the meaning and the truth of any idea is a function of its practical outcome.

LABEL: precision (semantic)
DEFINITION: The degree of refinement or specificity applied to a particular semantic categorization.
EXAMPLE: "Car repair manual" is a more semantically precise term than "document," even though both may be equally accurate.

LABEL: predicate
DEFINITION: A statement you can make about something that can be evaluated later as true or false.

LABEL: prime
DEFINITION: Types which are atomic and have no supertypes. There is a belief that there are a few semantic primes from which all business-related applications can be built.

LABEL: property
DEFINITION: An attribute (Datatype) or relationship (ObjectType) of an object/individual.

LABEL: property
DEFINITION: In object-oriented design, either an attribute or a relationship.

LABEL: prototypes
DEFINITION: A way of defining categories around exemplar representatives.
EXAMPLE: A "robin" may be a prototype for the category "bird."

LABEL: query
DEFINITION: A declarative statement describing the dataset that a user or program wants to obtain from a database.

LABEL: query
DEFINITION: To request information from a data store.

LABEL: range
DEFINITION: A restricted set of the domain of values to which an attribute can belong.

LABEL: range
DEFINITION: Restriction class for a property. See slot and domain (ontology).

LABEL: reachable
DEFINITION: The set of all nodes in a graph that can be arrived at by traversing arcs.

LABEL: real-time
DEFINITION: System design where events in the computer are taking place at nearly the same clock time as in the real world.

CONCEPT: really simple syndication/rdf site summary/rich site summary
LABEL: really simple syndication/rdf site summary/rich site summary
DEFINITION: A family of standards for bloggers and content syndication.

LABEL: reasoner
DEFINITION: A software program that can assign members to classes based on formal class definitions.

LABEL: recursive
DEFINITION: Flow of control in which a module calls a new instance of itself an indefinite number of times. See recursive.

LABEL: referent
DEFINITION: The real world object which an individual represents in an ontology.
EXAMPLE: “Horse” is a symbol, which stands for a concept. The referent is what kicks you.

LABEL: referential integrity
DEFINITION: Property of database management system that allows it to manage the relationship of instances in different tables such that a change or deletion in one table does not invalidate information in another. Referential integrity would prevent the deletion of a customer if there were still orders outstanding for that customer.

LABEL: reification
DEFINITION: Statements that refer to other RDF statements. For instance, to make a reference that another assertion is false or dubious is a reification.

LABEL: reify
DEFINITION: To treat an abstraction as if it were real.
EXAMPLE: Marriage is the reification of a relationship, as are most entities in most databases.

LABEL: repository
DEFINITION: Place to persistently store metadata. A database for metadata.

LABEL: resource
DEFINITION: In RDF terms, a URI or a literal.

LABEL: resource description framework
DEFINITION: Basic model for expressing knowledge in the Semantic Web.

LABEL: resource description framework schema
DEFINITION: Adds schema properties to RDF, such as "subclass" and "inverse."

LABEL: restriction
DEFINITION: A class definition where membership can be inferred based on precise definitions of membership qualification.

LABEL: run time
DEFINITION: Refers to things which can change when the program is running as opposed to those things which must be changed when the program is being designed (or compiled). Shifting things (e.g., hardware, software, data) from design time to run time can make the system much more flexible.

LABEL: schema
DEFINITION: Allowable tags and their sequencing, usually expressed in DTD or XSD.

LABEL: schema
DEFINITION: Data definition for tables.

LABEL: semantic
DEFINITION: Concerned with the study of meaning (often the meaning of words). In business systems we are concerned with making the meaning of data explicit (structuring unstructured data), as well as making it explicit enough that an agent could reason about it.

CONCEPT: Semantic Annotations for Web Services Description Language
LABEL: Semantic Annotations for Web Services Description Language
DEFINITION: Standard for adding semantic description of Web service capability as annotation in the WSDL interface definition. (Previously, WSDL-S)

LABEL: semantic data modeling
DEFINITION: Conceptual database modeling based on semantics.

LABEL: Semantic Web
DEFINITION: Next generation  Internet where all the content is tagged with semantic tags and committed to ontologies. An interlinking of ontologies will allow agents to reason about information only tangentially connected (and not previously connected by their creators).

CONCEPT: Semantics in Business Vocabulary and Business Rules
LABEL: Semantics in Business Vocabulary and Business Rules
DEFINITION: A meta model and standard vocabulary for specifying business rules.

LABEL: semiotics
DEFINITION: A branch of linguistics primarily concerned with human use of sign, symbol, syntax, and semantics.

LABEL: sentient
DEFINITION: Capable of reasoning. Alternative definition includes being capable of feeling, but that has no applicability for business systems.

LABEL: service-oriented architecture
DEFINITION: Application architecture organized around the use of services, including Web services.

LABEL: service-oriented integration
DEFINITION: Performing EAI using service-based technologies.

LABEL: shredding
DEFINITION: Parsing an XML document to is constituent parts to be stored atomically in a relational database.

LABEL: similarity
DEFINITION: Lexical relations of words with related meaning. For example, "gluttonous" is similar to "greedy."

LABEL: simple HTML ontology extension
DEFINITION: An early project to extend HTML with semantic tags.

LABEL: Simple Knowledge Organization System
DEFINITION: A standard for describing knowledge structures such as taxonomies and thesauri.

LABEL: simple object access protocol
DEFINITION: Wrapper for Web service requests that allows them to be invoked across the  Internet, including through firewalls.

LABEL: slot
DEFINITION: A property in an ontology that can refer to other terms or frames.

LABEL: sophists
DEFINITION: A group of philosophers who believed that the world existed only to the extent it was perceived. "Man is the measure of all things" was a saying of the sophists.

LABEL: SPARQL
DEFINITION: Query language for RDF data.

LABEL: specialization
DEFINITION: Increasing semantic precision by subtyping. Almost an exact antonym to generalization, but there are a few obscure conditions where generalization and specialization are not inverses.

LABEL: splitters
DEFINITION: People who are inclined to create new categories whenever new distinctions come up.

LABEL: standard generalized markup language
DEFINITION: Early tagged document markup language. Was popular for complex document creation, but complexity of language led to it being largely superceded by HTML and XML.

LABEL: subsumption
DEFINITION: To classify, include or incorporate in a more comprehensive category or under a general principle. The "isa" relationship.

LABEL: subtype
DEFINITION: A proper subtype "is" one of its parent types, more specifically a specialization of that type.

LABEL: suggested upper merged ontology
DEFINITION: A broad ontology meant to promote wide ranging interoperability, supported by IEEE.

LABEL: swoRDFish
DEFINITION: Ontology and framework for managing digital assets, from Sun Microsystems.

LABEL: syllogism
DEFINITION: A style of inductive logic, that starts with a generalization, includes a categorization and concludes with a semantic entailment or the instance taking on an attribute of the category.
EXAMPLE: All men are mortal (generalization). Socrates is a man (categorization). Socrates is mortal (XXX).

LABEL: symbolic
DEFINITION: Semantic reasoning with variables substituted for semantically known objects. Conclusions drawn at this level are universally true.

LABEL: symmetric
DEFINITION: Characteristic of a property which has it hold “both ways.”
EXAMPLE: “Sibling” is a symmetric property, but “sister” is not.

LABEL: synchronous
DEFINITION: Message transmission where sender blocks and waits for reply, which is expected in near real time.

LABEL: synonymy
DEFINITION: Two terms that mean the same thing. As pointed out by John Saeed*, there are few true synonyms.

LABEL: syntactic
DEFINITION: Concerning the grammar order or special characters in a document or message.

LABEL: tacit
DEFINITION: That which has not been expressed in formal terms. Tacit knowledge may be knowledge we have without knowing that we have it.

LABEL: tag
DEFINITION: Delimiters that also contain information. Most common type are matched tags such as <t>42</t>, which is the number 42 tagged by the tag "t."

LABEL: taxonomy
DEFINITION: A vocabulary ordered into a hierarchy, generally to find terms easily, and also to subtype the terms.

LABEL: temporal
DEFINITION: Dealing with time.
EXAMPLE: Events, plans

LABEL: terminology box
DEFINITION: Inference that can be done with the Terminology (metadata) layer only.
NOTE: TBox statements are sometimes associated with object-oriented classes and ABox statements associated with instances of those classes.

LABEL: text
DEFINITION: A portion of a document expressed in characters (as opposed to sound or graphics).

LABEL: thing
DEFINITION: Very often the top of a generalization tree.

LABEL: Tim Berners-Lee
DEFINITION: WWW inventor; often goes by his initials.

LABEL: transactive
DEFINITION: A characteristic of a property which allows it to be recursive.
EXAMPLE: “Ancestor” is a transitive property, but “parent” is not.

LABEL: tree
DEFINITION: A directed graph in which nodes are not referred to by more than one node.
NOTE: Children do not have more than one parent.

LABEL: triple
DEFINITION: A single combination of Subject/Predicate/Object.

LABEL: triple
DEFINITION: Knowledge expressed in a three-part grammar, which has been called "subject, predicate, object" as well as “resource, property, values."

LABEL: triple store
DEFINITION: A database that stores RDF in its native form.

LABEL: truth conditions
DEFINITION: The conditions under which a sentence or a proposition expressed by it is true;
EXAMPLE: The statement “I have red hair” is true under the condition that the speaker has, in fact, red hair. It is not true in the abstract, but only when grounded.

LABEL: unambiguous
DEFINITION: Refers to specific item or category in requisite level of semantic precision.

LABEL: unary
DEFINITION: One-way relation; pointer.Most relations are binary, which means they are automatically maintained both ways and can be traversed both ways.

LABEL: unicode
DEFINITION: Character set rich enough to represent non-Latin-based languages, such as Chinese and Burmese.

LABEL: unified medical language system
DEFINITION: Ontology of medical terms used for searching medical literature.

LABEL: unified modeling language
DEFINITION: Modeling language for object-oriented development popularized by Rational Corporation.

LABEL: uniform resource identifier
DEFINITION: Unambiguous location of a resource in RDF.

LABEL: uniform resource location
DEFINITION: A resolvable location on the reachable  Internet.

LABEL: unique
DEFINITION: There can not be more than one equivalent item of this type within the scope indicated. We may say that customer numbers must be unique (within our organization or database) or we may say that there can only be one successor on a relationship, meaning there can't be more than one of that type in that set.

LABEL: universal description, discovery, and integration
DEFINITION: Standard for a registry or yellow pages for finding services.

LABEL: unstructured data
DEFINITION: Data (textual, video, sound, graphics) that has not been interpreted, tagged, or structured.

LABEL: valence
DEFINITION: Number of type of successors to a relationship. Also called the "n-arity." Most relationships have a valence of 2 (binary relationships), but relationships with a valence of 3 or 4 are not uncommon.

LABEL: validation
DEFINITION: Determination that a document obeys all the rules set out in its schema.

LABEL: veracity
DEFINITION: Degree to which we believe something to be true.
EXAMPLE: High veracity = high degree in belief in the truth of the assertion.

LABEL: vocabulary
DEFINITION: List of terms in a particular dialect, often with definitions.

LABEL: warehouses
DEFINITION: A copy of the operational data of a firm, stored to optimize analytic retrieval instead of updates. Also organized to be robust in regard to changes in the structure of the operational databases or the hierarchical rollups of the dimensions.

LABEL: Web 2.0
DEFINITION: Web based capability characterized by collaboration and user-created content, including blogs and wikis.

LABEL: Web ontology language
DEFINITION: Successor to DAML + OIL a W3C standard.
NOTE: The origin of the dyslexic acronym is attributed to the owl in Winnie the Pooh who spelled his name "WOL."

LABEL: Web services
DEFINITION: RPC in which the request is in XML. Allows caller and receiver to be in different technologies as long as each can queue the message and process the XML request or response.

LABEL: well formedness
DEFINITION: Property that a given tagged document adheres to the rules of documents of that type (e.g., all the tags match). Does not require a schema. See validation. Note that most HTML tools and browsers have become slack on well formedness, to the point where one cannot rely on HTML tags matching.

LABEL: WordNet
DEFINITION: Open source dictionary of the English language. Built as a searchable graph with disambiguation of word senses and thesaurus-style linking of similar word senses. Many of the concepts have hypernymy, polysymy, and mereologic links.

LABEL: World Wide Web
DEFINITION: The layer on top of the Internet that most people now think of as the Internet. Includes Web servers that are reachable by URLs and DNS, that accept HTTP reuqests on port 80 and that serve up user Interfaces in HTML.

LABEL: World Wide Web Consortium
DEFINITION: Non profit organization responsible for maintaining the standards upon which the World Wide Web is based.

LABEL: WSDL
DEFINITION: Standard for defining the interface to a Web service, expressed as an XSD dialect. Pronounced "whizdull."

LABEL: XMI
DEFINITION: Standard for interchanging metadata.

LABEL: XML schema
DEFINITION: Schema language for XML, expressed in XML (as opposed to DTD, which was not in XML).

LABEL: XML style sheet language
DEFINITION: Declarative language creating a style sheet for XML documents.

LABEL: XPath
DEFINITION: Declarative way to define a subset of an XML document that you are interested in. Robust in regard to many structural changes to the document.

LABEL: XQuery
DEFINITION: Query language for retrieving data from an XML document or XML database.
